subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 35 minutes × 1 period = 35 minutes
Total: 1 periods · 35 minutes

periods.activity_title: Which Objects Spin? Observe and Record
periods.textbook_anchor: How Things Work — observe and record which objects spin and which do not (p. 105)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook table for recording spin observations (p. 105)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the opening story of Meera and Dhruv aloud; students share one object from daily life they have seen spinning.
Students individually list objects they think can spin and those they think cannot, then share briefly with a partner.

In pairs, students collect the six objects (coin, bangle, pencil, stone, wooden top, eraser), spin each one, and record observations in the textbook table — noting whether it spins well, briefly, or not at all.
Class discussion: Which objects spun well? What do those objects have in common? Students share observations aloud.
Teacher draws out the idea of shape and balance affecting spinning; students note one finding in their own words.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record whether physical objects behave consistently under the same action, and identify a pattern across multiple trials.
periods.section_context: Spinning behaviour of coin, bangle, pencil, stone, wooden top, eraser.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did anything surprise you — an object you thought would spin well but didn't?' Encourage students to connect to traditional spinning objects they may have seen at home or in their community, such as a lattu or a chakri toy, letting that conversation arise naturally from their responses.

periods.textbook_anchor: How Things Work — make spinners with centred and off-centre holes, spin and record observations (p. 106)

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows the textbook spinner diagrams; students predict which spinner they think will spin best and why.
In groups of three, students construct at least two spinners — one with the toothpick through the centre and one with the toothpick off-centre — following textbook configurations.
Students test each spinner, observe how long and how steadily it spins, and record observations in a simple table in their notebooks.
Groups discuss: Which spinner did not spin properly? What could be the reason? Students refer to the discuss prompts on p. 108.
Teacher consolidates: the position of the axle relative to the centre of the shape determines spinning quality.

periods.implied_lo: Students can test how changing a single variable in a constructed object affects its functional behaviour, and record observations systematically.
periods.section_context: Cardboard spinners with centred vs. off-centre toothpick axles; spinner shape variations.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Pose: 'If you moved the toothpick just a little away from the centre, what do you think would happen?' Prompt groups to colour their best-spinning spinner with two or three colours and observe what happens to the colours during rotation, connecting naturally to how a charkha wheel appears when it spins fast.

periods.activity_title: Predict, Test, and Discuss: Float or Sink?
periods.textbook_anchor: Floating and Sinking — predict and test whether objects float or sink in water (p. 110)
materials: bucket or large basin with water

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Meera-Dhruv paper-boat scene; students recall a time they saw something float or sink unexpectedly.
Students individually fill in their predictions (F/S) for each object in the textbook table before any testing begins.
In groups, students drop each object into the water basin and record the actual result (F/S) beside their prediction.
Class discussion: Did all heavy objects sink and all light objects float? Students name exceptions and try to explain them.
Teacher poses the key question for next period: 'Can we make something float just by changing its shape?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can make and compare predictions about physical outcomes against observed results, and identify cases where an expected pattern does not hold.
periods.section_context: Leaf, iron nail, empty katori, plastic bottle, stone, aluminium foil — float or sink prediction and testing.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why do you think the empty katori floated even though it is heavier than the leaf?' Accept all reasoning; the goal is productive uncertainty, not the correct answer yet. If students mention paper boats or coconut-shell boats from home experience, encourage them to share.

periods.activity_title: Shape Changes Everything: Aluminium Foil Experiment
periods.textbook_anchor: Floating and Sinking — test aluminium foil in spread-out, ball, and cup shapes; record F or S and reason (p. 112)
materials: aluminium foil (three equal pieces per group)

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps previous finding: weight alone doesn't decide. Introduces question: 'What if we change only the shape but keep the material the same?'

Groups take three identical pieces of aluminium foil, shape them as instructed (spread out flat, pressed into a tight ball, folded into a cup), drop each into water, and record F or S plus their reason in the table on p. 112.
Groups share results; teacher facilitates comparison — all three pieces were the same material and same amount, yet different outcomes.
Students write one sentence in their notebooks explaining why shape affects floating or sinking, using their own words.
Teacher connects to boat design: 'What shape would you use if you wanted to build a boat that carries the most weight?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can isolate shape as a variable and demonstrate how the same material produces different physical outcomes when its form changes.
periods.section_context: Aluminium foil in three shapes — spread out flat, compressed ball, cup — floating and sinking.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If a cup shape floats, what happens if we press the sides down slowly — when does it start to sink?' Encourage students to test this if time permits. Let the conversation move naturally to how traditional boat builders (using coconut shells or folded leaves) understood shape without formal science.

periods.textbook_anchor: Floating and Sinking — design, draw, and construct a boat from local materials; organise class exhibition (p. 113)

time_bands.activity: Groups of 3–4 students discuss boat design using available materials; each student sketches their boat idea and the group agrees on one plan.
Groups build their boats, ensuring their design differs from other groups'; teacher circulates and asks groups to explain their design choices.
Each boat is tested in the water basin; groups observe and note strengths and challenges in the comparison table on p. 114.
Brief gallery walk — groups look at others' boats and note one strength of another group's design before the class exhibition is formally opened.

periods.implied_lo: Students can apply understanding of shape and material properties to design, build, and evaluate a functional object, and communicate their reasoning to others.
periods.section_context: Boat construction using paper, cardboard, ice-cream sticks, clay; class exhibition and comparison table.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask each group: 'What was the most important decision you made in your design?' During the gallery walk, prompt students to connect their designs to any traditional boat forms they know — walnut-shell boats, coconut-shell floats — without labelling these as special knowledge.

periods.activity_title: Comparing and Reflecting on Boat Designs
periods.textbook_anchor: Floating and Sinking — compare boats and record strengths and challenges in the table (p. 114)

time_bands.activity: Each group presents their boat for 1–2 minutes: materials used, design choice, and one thing they would change if they built it again.
Students individually complete the textbook comparison table: strengths and challenges of their own boat versus at least one other group's boat.
Whole-class discussion: What design features made some boats stronger or more stable? Students connect back to the aluminium foil experiment — how shape matters.
Teacher facilitates a brief reflection: 'People across the world have made boats from what was around them — bark, reeds, shells. What materials near your home could you use?'
Students write one sentence: the most important thing they learned about floating and sinking from the boat challenge.

periods.implied_lo: Students can compare the functional outcomes of different design choices, identify strengths and limitations, and connect material-and-shape reasoning to real-world contexts.
periods.section_context: Comparing student-built boats; recording strengths and challenges; linking shape and material to floating.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did any group's boat surprise you — either floating better or worse than you expected? Why?' Encourage students to articulate the connection between shape and buoyancy in their own words rather than confirming a teacher-provided explanation.

periods.activity_title: Framing Questions and Reasoning About Balance
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — frame inquiry questions about a spinning phenomenon; reason about a hanging mobile balance (p. 115)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure of unbalanced hanging mobile (p. 115)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the scenario of Ravi's spinning observation aloud; students think silently and write at least two questions Ravi could ask his teacher.
Pairs share their questions; class lists the best questions on the board and discusses what kind of investigation could answer each one.
Teacher shows the textbook mobile figure (p. 115); students examine it and write their answer to what should be done to balance the mobile bending towards side A.
Class discussion: What does it mean for something to be balanced? How does this connect to the spinners from Period 2 — why does a centred axle help a spinner stay steady?
Students note one connection between balance and spinning in their notebooks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can formulate testable inquiry questions about an observed phenomenon and apply reasoning about balance to explain a physical scenario.
periods.section_context: Ravi's spinner slowing down — inquiry question framing; hanging mobile balance figure.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: For the question-framing task, prompt: 'A good question is one you could actually test — does your question pass that test?' For the mobile, avoid giving the answer; instead ask: 'Which side is heavier? What would make the other side heavier?'

periods.activity_title: Classify, Reason, and Reflect on Float and Sink
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — classify everyday objects as floaters or sinkers; reason about changing float/sink behaviour (p. 115–116)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook list of objects for classification (p. 116)

time_bands.activity: Students read the reflection question on p. 115: How would you make a floating object sink and a sinking object float? They write their individual answers before any discussion.

Students classify the fourteen objects on p. 116 (wax, marble, thermocol, candle, coin, cork, leaf, eraser, spoon, ice-cube, potato, tomato, pumpkin, lemon) into floaters and sinkers using reasoning — not physical testing.
Pairs compare their classifications and discuss any disagreements; teacher highlights contested items (ice-cube, lemon, potato) and asks: 'What makes you uncertain?'
Whole-class consolidation: students revisit their earlier predictions from Period 3 and reflect — what do they now know that they did not know at the start of the chapter?
Students write one sentence about what they would investigate next if they could design their own experiment, closing the chapter on an open, curious note.

periods.implied_lo: Students can apply criteria developed through investigation to classify unfamiliar objects, and articulate how their reasoning has changed as a result of inquiry.
periods.section_context: Classifying wax, marble, thermocol, candle, coin, cork, leaf, eraser, spoon, ice-cube, potato, tomato, pumpkin, lemon as floaters or sinkers.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'For the objects you were unsure about, what information would help you decide?' Draw attention to how students' thinking has shifted across the chapter — from guessing to reasoning — making the growth in scientific thinking visible and worth celebrating.

assessment_items.question_text: Meera and Dhruv spun six objects — a coin, a bangle, a pencil, a stone, a wooden top, and an eraser. They spun each object three times and recorded what happened each time. What is the BEST reason for spinning each object more than once before writing down a result?

options.label: A
options.text: To check whether the same object behaves consistently across multiple tries and to find a pattern in the results.

options.label: B
options.text: To make the object spin faster each time by giving it more practice.

options.label: C
options.text: To count how many times the object spins before it stops.

options.label: D
options.text: To give every student in the group a turn to spin the object.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. This item assesses whether students understood the purpose of repeated observation — finding consistent patterns — which is the core scientific practice modelled in Period 1's spinning activity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record whether physical objects behave consistently under the same action, and identify a pattern across multiple trials.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates a misconception that repeated spinning trains or improves the object — confuses practice with observation for consistency.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates the student conflates duration of spinning with identifying a reliable pattern — a partial understanding of what to record.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates the student is focused on procedural fairness in group work rather than the scientific purpose of repeated trials.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya made two cardboard spinners of the same size and shape. In Spinner 1, she pushed the toothpick axle through the centre of the cardboard. In Spinner 2, she pushed the toothpick axle through a point near the edge of the cardboard. She spun both spinners and wrote in her notebook: 'Spinner 1 spun smoothly for a long time. Spinner 2 wobbled and fell over quickly.' Using what you discovered during the spinner-making activity, explain why the two spinners behaved differently.
expected_elements: Identification that Spinner 1 has its axle at the centre, making it balanced.
Identification that Spinner 2 has its axle off-centre, making it unbalanced.
Explanation that an off-centre axle causes uneven distribution around the pivot point, leading to wobbling and early stopping.
Connection to the variable that was changed: position of the hole (axle position) is the single variable that differed between the two spinners.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any age-appropriate phrasing that conveys balance/imbalance due to axle position. Students need not use technical vocabulary like 'centre of mass'; responses like 'one side is heavier than the other' or 'the cardboard is not equal on all sides' are acceptable and sufficient.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can test how changing a single variable in a constructed object affects its functional behaviour, and record observations systematically.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Identification that Spinner 1 has its axle at the centre, making it balanced.
Identification that Spinner 2 has its axle off-centre, making it unbalanced.
Explanation that an off-centre axle causes uneven distribution around the pivot point, leading to wobbling and early stopping.
Connection to the variable that was changed: position of the hole (axle position) is the single variable that differed between the two spinners.

assessment_items.question_text: During the float-and-sink activity, your class tested a leaf, an iron nail, an empty katori, a plastic bottle, a stone, and aluminium foil in water. Before testing, most students predicted that heavy objects will sink and light objects will float. After testing, some predictions turned out to be wrong. Name ONE object from the list above whose result surprised you (or your class), and explain why its behaviour did not match the prediction based on weight alone.
expected_elements: Naming a specific object from the listed set whose actual result differed from the weight-based prediction (e.g., empty katori — heavy but floats; iron nail — relatively small but sinks; aluminium foil — light but can sink when balled up).
Stating what the weight-based prediction would have been for that object.
Describing what actually happened when the object was placed in water.
Recognising that weight alone is not a reliable predictor of floating or sinking — at least one other factor (such as shape or whether it is hollow) matters.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any valid object from the listed set whose behaviour counters weight-only reasoning. The empty katori and the iron nail are the most commonly cited surprises in this activity. Full marks require both identifying the unexpected result and articulating why weight alone did not predict it.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can make and compare predictions about physical outcomes against observed results, and identify cases where an expected pattern does not hold.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

Describing what actually happened when the object was placed in water.

assessment_items.question_text: In the aluminium foil activity, Arjun used three equal-sized pieces of the same aluminium foil. He shaped them differently: Piece 1 — spread out flat; Piece 2 — pressed tightly into a ball; Piece 3 — shaped like a small cup. He tested each in water. Piece 1 floated, Piece 2 sank, and Piece 3 floated. Which conclusion is BEST supported by Arjun's results?

options.label: A
options.text: The shape of an object affects whether it floats or sinks, even when the material is exactly the same.

options.label: B
options.text: Aluminium always floats in water because it is a light metal.

options.label: C
options.text: Only the weight of the object decides whether it will float or sink.

options.label: D
options.text: The size of the piece of foil is what caused the difference in floating and sinking.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. This item directly tests whether students isolated shape as the variable explaining different outcomes in the foil activity. All three pieces were identical in material and size, so only shape changed.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can isolate shape as a variable and demonstrate how the same material produces different physical outcomes when its form changes.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates a misconception that aluminium inherently floats — the student has not registered that Piece 2 (ball shape) sank, showing material alone does not determine outcome.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Indicates the student is still holding the prior misconception that weight determines floating/sinking, which this activity was designed to challenge.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates confusion about the controlled variable — the student has not registered that all three pieces were of equal size, so size cannot be the cause.

assessment_items.task:
Your group has designed and built a boat using materials available in the classroom (paper, cardboard, ice-cream sticks, clay, tape, or others you chose). Now, test your boat in water. Then complete the two tasks below:

Task A — Draw your boat and label the materials you used and where you used them.
Task B — Write two sentences: (1) One thing your boat does well (a strength). (2) One thing that did not work as well as you hoped (a challenge), and what you think caused it.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Use this structure to organise your response:
• My boat is made of: [list your materials]
• My boat [floated / sank / tipped over] when placed in water.
• Strength: My boat was good at _____ because _____.
• Challenge: My boat did not _____ well because _____.
• If I could change one thing, I would _____ because _____.
format_of_output: Labelled drawing of the boat showing materials used
Two written sentences identifying one strength and one challenge with a reason for each
assessment_items.annotation: Assess the quality of the student's reasoning about their own design choices — especially whether they connect material and shape to the boat's behaviour in water. A boat that sank is not a failure if the student can reason clearly about why. Accept all locally available materials; there is no single correct design.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can apply understanding of shape and material properties to design, build, and evaluate a functional object, and communicate their reasoning to others.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

guide.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can link the properties of chosen materials and the shape of their design to the boat's observed behaviour in water, and communicate that reasoning clearly — the core application goal of the boat-building activity.
guide.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold is a support, not a checklist. A student who writes fluently without it should not be penalised. The scaffold helps students who struggled to start; the quality of reasoning in the strength/challenge sentences is what matters, not adherence to the sentence frame.
guide.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: The student names specific materials, explains how shape or material choice contributed to the boat's behaviour, and identifies a genuine causal reason for the challenge (e.g., 'the clay made one side heavy so the boat tipped'). Weak: The student lists materials without connecting them to floating/sinking, or gives a challenge without any reason (e.g., 'my boat sank' with no explanation).
guide.inclusivity: Students who are stronger in drawing than writing may submit a richly labelled diagram with minimal written sentences — accept if the labels convey material-and-shape reasoning. Students who cannot draw representationally may describe their boat in words alone. Both pathways demonstrate the same underlying understanding.
guide.format_type: Labelled drawing plus short written reflection
guide.format_rationale: The C&E dominant mode requires a created product and communicative output. The labelled drawing makes design thinking visible; the written sentences demand evaluative reasoning. Together they match the implied_lo's requirement to both build and communicate reasoning.

assessment_items.question_text:
After the class boat exhibition, each group looked at every other group's boat and filled in a comparison table of strengths and challenges. Look at the two boats described below and answer the question that follows.

Boat A: Made of cardboard with clay pressed around the base. It floated but tilted to one side.
Boat B: Made of thick cardboard folded into a box shape with tape sealing the sides. It floated upright and held a small stone inside without sinking.

Using what you learned about shape and materials from the floating-and-sinking activities, explain why Boat B performed better than Boat A. In your answer, mention at least one strength of Boat B's design and one reason Boat A had a problem.
look_for: Identifies a specific design feature of Boat B that contributed to its success — e.g., the enclosed box shape traps air and distributes weight evenly, keeping it upright.
Identifies a specific problem with Boat A's design — e.g., clay concentrated weight unevenly at the base or on one side, causing tilting.
Uses the concept of shape mattering for floating from the foil activity — explicitly or implicitly connects shape to outcome.
Uses the concept that the same material behaves differently depending on how it is used or distributed — connecting material-and-shape reasoning to real boat design.
Goes beyond description to a reasoned explanation (not just 'Boat B is better' but 'because the box shape/sealed sides/even weight distribution allowed it to stay upright').
assessment_items.annotation: This item rewards transfer from the foil-shape experiment to a real design scenario. Award full marks for responses that give a causal explanation grounded in shape and/or material distribution, even if phrasing is simple. Partial marks for responses that correctly identify a feature or problem but do not explain the causal link.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare the functional outcomes of different design choices, identify strengths and limitations, and connect material-and-shape reasoning to real-world contexts.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with disciplinary core ideas in the natural sciences, as well as in engineering, technology, and applications of science, which reflect the content that will be learned across subject areas in later Grades

look_for: Identifies a specific design feature of Boat B that contributed to its success — e.g., the enclosed box shape traps air and distributes weight evenly, keeping it upright.
Identifies a specific problem with Boat A's design — e.g., clay concentrated weight unevenly at the base or on one side, causing tilting.
Uses the concept of shape mattering for floating from the foil activity — explicitly or implicitly connects shape to outcome.
Uses the concept that the same material behaves differently depending on how it is used or distributed — connecting material-and-shape reasoning to real boat design.
Goes beyond description to a reasoned explanation (not just 'Boat B is better' but 'because the box shape/sealed sides/even weight distribution allowed it to stay upright').

assessment_items.question_text:
Ravi spins a spinner and notices it slows down and eventually stops. He wants to ask his science teacher questions to find out why this happens.

Part A: Write TWO questions that Ravi could ask his teacher about why the spinner slows down and stops. Make sure your questions could actually be tested or investigated.

Part B: Look at a mobile (a hanging decoration) that is tilting down on side A. Write ONE thing that could be done to make the mobile balance again.
expected_elements: Part A — Question 1: A question that identifies a testable factor related to spinner slowing — e.g., 'Does the surface the spinner spins on affect how long it keeps spinning?', 'Does the size of the spinner change how long it spins?', 'Does the weight of the spinner affect how quickly it stops?', or 'Does air around the spinner slow it down?'
Part A — Question 2: A second, distinct testable question — not a repetition of the first — that identifies a different factor or aspect of the phenomenon.

Part B: A correct and specific adjustment — e.g., 'Add weight to side B', 'Move an object from side A to side B', 'Remove some weight from side A' — with at least a brief reason (e.g., 'to make both sides equal').
assessment_items.annotation: For Part A, accept any question that is genuinely testable and relevant to the spinner slowing-down phenomenon — do not require precise scientific vocabulary. Reject questions that are purely descriptive ('Why does it stop?') unless the student has framed it as investigable. For Part B, accept any answer that correctly identifies adding weight to the lighter side or removing weight from the heavier side as the solution.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can formulate testable inquiry questions about an observed phenomenon and apply reasoning about balance to explain a physical scenario.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

expected_elements: Part A — Question 1: A question that identifies a testable factor related to spinner slowing — e.g., 'Does the surface the spinner spins on affect how long it keeps spinning?', 'Does the size of the spinner change how long it spins?', 'Does the weight of the spinner affect how quickly it stops?', or 'Does air around the spinner slow it down?'
Part A — Question 2: A second, distinct testable question — not a repetition of the first — that identifies a different factor or aspect of the phenomenon.

Part B: A correct and specific adjustment — e.g., 'Add weight to side B', 'Move an object from side A to side B', 'Remove some weight from side A' — with at least a brief reason (e.g., 'to make both sides equal').

assessment_items.task:
Here is a list of everyday objects: Wax, Marble, Thermocol, Candle, Coin, Cork, Leaf, Eraser, Spoon, Ice-cube, Potato, Tomato, Pumpkin, Lemon.

Step 1 — Classify: Sort all fourteen objects into two groups — Floaters and Sinkers — using what you have learned during this chapter about shape, material, and weight.

Step 2 — Justify: Choose TWO objects from your list that you think most students would get wrong (one from the Floaters group and one from the Sinkers group). For each, write one sentence explaining why it ends up in that group even though it might seem surprising.

Step 3 — Reflect: Write two to three sentences describing how your thinking about floating and sinking has changed from the beginning of this chapter to now.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Floaters: _______________________________________________
Sinkers: _______________________________________________

Surprising Floater: [object] floats because _____.
Surprising Sinker: [object] sinks because _____.

At the start of this chapter, I thought _____.
Now I know that _____.
This changed because _____.
format_of_output: Two-column classification table or list (Floaters and Sinkers) with all fourteen objects placed
Two justification sentences identifying and explaining surprising placements
A three-sentence reflection on how the student's thinking changed
assessment_items.annotation: Standard expected classifications — Floaters: Wax, Thermocol, Cork, Leaf, Ice-cube, Tomato, Pumpkin, Lemon, Candle (most); Sinkers: Marble, Coin, Eraser, Spoon, Potato. Note: Lemon and potato are borderline and regionally familiar objects — lemon typically floats, potato typically sinks, but results may vary slightly with variety or water salinity. Accept well-reasoned alternative placements for borderline objects. The reflection (Step 3) is assessed on evidence of genuine conceptual shift — not on correctness of self-report. Teacher note: Regionally varied answers are acceptable for objects like lemon and potato, where local varieties may produce different results; credit clear reasoning regardless of final placement.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can apply criteria developed through investigation to classify unfamiliar objects, and articulate how their reasoning has changed as a result of inquiry.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

guide.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can transfer the shape-and-material reasoning built across the chapter's investigations to classify a new set of objects, identify genuinely surprising cases, and articulate a conceptual shift — the R&A period's core reflective and applicative demand.
guide.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold supports students who find open classification daunting. Students who produce a fluent, well-organised response without the scaffold should receive full credit. The three-step structure is the intellectual demand; the scaffold is the access route.
guide.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: Correct or well-reasoned classification of most objects; justification sentences that invoke shape, material density, or hollow-vs-solid reasoning (not just 'it is light'); a reflection that shows a genuine shift from weight-only thinking to multi-factor reasoning. Weak: Classification based purely on weight or size; justification sentences that simply restate the outcome ('it floats because it floats'); a reflection that is generic ('I learned a lot') without identifying a specific conceptual change.
guide.inclusivity: Students who struggle with written expression may draw the two-column table and dictate their justification and reflection sentences to the teacher or a peer scribe. Students who can demonstrate their classification orally during a brief teacher check-in should be credited if written output is challenging. Both modes access the same reasoning.
guide.format_type: Two-column classification list, two written justification sentences, and a short written reflection
guide.format_rationale: The R&A dominant mode requires the student to apply accumulated reasoning to new cases and to articulate metacognitive change. The classification list makes the application visible and checkable; the justification sentences demand causal reasoning; the reflection sentences demand metacognitive articulation — together they match the full implied_lo.
